Adaptive Loss-Weighting for PINNs 1D Allen-Cahn benchmark

Comparing four loss-weighting strategies for physics-informed neural networks on a stiff reaction-diffusion equation, plus a stiffness sweep that uncovered a benchmark-design pitfall.

Problem Methods Results Predictions Stiffness sweep Discussion

The benchmark

The Allen-Cahn equation models phase separation and is a standard PINN stress-test because its solution develops sharp transition layers that a smooth neural network can easily under-resolve.

u_t = ε² u_xx + u − u³,   x ∈ [−1, 1], t ∈ [0, 1]   |   u(x,0) = x²cos(πx)   |   periodic BC, ε = 0.1

Four weighting strategies

1. Baseline

Vanilla PINN: unweighted sum of residual + IC + BC mean-squared losses.

2. Gradient-norm balancing

Every 200 steps, rescale IC/BC weights so their parameter-gradient magnitude matches the residual term's, via an exponential moving average.

3. Self-adaptive (SA-PINN)

Every collocation/IC/BC point gets its own trainable weight, updated by gradient ascent alongside the network's gradient descent (a min-max objective), following McClenny & Braga-Neto (2020).

4. Self-adaptive + RAD

Same as (3), plus residual-based adaptive resampling: every 1,000 steps, collocation points are resampled toward regions of currently-high residual.

The stiffness sweep: a surprise finding

To resolve a contradiction with the original SA-PINN paper (which reports self-adaptive weighting winning by a wide margin on this exact benchmark), we swept eps across 5 more values spanning 3 further orders of magnitude.

Why: the initial condition u(x,0)=x²cos(πx) places a broad central region right at the PDE's unstable equilibrium (u=0). Escaping it requires a diffusion-driven nudge whose delay saturates below eps≈0.01 — so within our t∈[0,1] window, the true solution simply stops changing as eps shrinks further.

This is a benchmark-design lesson: a stiffness-parameter sweep is only informative if the ground-truth solution actually changes character as the parameter shrinks. For this initial condition and time horizon, it doesn't — so a flat method comparison here reflects the benchmark's construction, not the weighting methods. We haven't found this specific saturation effect flagged elsewhere in the PINN weighting literature.

A second, more mundane factor likely also contributes to the original discrepancy: the literature's Allen-Cahn equation uses a 5×-rescaled reaction term (u_t − 0.0001u_xx + 5u³ − 5u = 0), not just a different eps — a true replication needs to match that exact equation, which we flag as the clearest remaining next step.

Discussion & limitations

Honest negative result (eps=0.1): both self-adaptive variants underperformed the simpler baseline and gradient-norm methods, contrary to the original SA-PINN paper.
  • Self-adaptive weight learning rate (1e-2) was not independently tuned.
  • 6,000-step training budget is short relative to typical published PINN work.
  • The stiffness-sweep saturation is specific to this initial condition and time horizon — a different IC or longer horizon would plausibly restore eps-sensitivity.
  • The literature's exact (5×-rescaled) equation was not yet replicated.
